plans.title: Anger
plans.intro: In 2.62 and 2.63 the Gita traces anger step by step: dwelling on something becomes attachment, attachment becomes wanting, blocked wanting becomes anger, and anger takes judgement with it. These verses walk that chain slowly, then turn to the steady mind, riding out the surge (5.23) and speech that doesn't wound (17.15). The last is from the Ramayana, a sage who lost his temper, lost years of work, and began again. This plan is for the anger you want to stop acting on. If someone is harming you, you are right to name it.

days.heading: Where anger starts
days.for_you: Krishna starts earlier than the outburst. Dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ: when you keep dwelling on something, you get attached, attachment turns into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall turns into anger. By the time you snap, the fire has been building for a while.
days.today: After your next flash of irritation, trace it back one step: what were you dwelling on?

days.heading: What anger takes from you
days.for_you: From anger comes confusion, then memory slips, then judgement goes, and then you fall. Krishna's word for that last step is praṇaśyati. You say the thing you can't take back, because the part of you that knew better has already left the room.
days.today: Recall one argument you regret. Find the moment judgement left. What came just before it?
days.note: Feeling anger is human. The warning is about anger that takes over your judgement.

days.heading: Know the real enemy
days.for_you: Arjuna asks why we do wrong against our own will. Krishna names desire, which turns into anger when it's blocked and is never satisfied. When you're angry at someone, look for what you wanted from them.
days.today: When you're angry today, finish this sentence: what I wanted was…

days.heading: A steady mind still feels
days.for_you: Krishna's portrait of the steady person: unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, free of clinging, fear and anger. This person still feels everything. The feelings just don't get to drive.
days.today: Picture the calmest person you know in your hardest situation. What would they do first?

days.heading: Ride out the surge
days.for_you: Krishna says whoever can withstand the surge (vega) of desire and anger, here in this life, is steady and happy. A surge rises and falls. Your only job is to wait until it passes before you act.
days.today: Next time the surge comes, let ten slow breaths pass before you speak or type.

days.heading: Then speak
days.for_you: Krishna calls it the discipline of speech: words that don't agitate, that are true, pleasant and helpful. Your anger often has a point. This verse shows how to make that point without cruelty, once the surge has passed.
days.today: Rewrite one message you sent in anger. Keep what's true. Drop what was meant to hurt.
days.note: Kind speech can still say hard things. It says them without cruelty.

days.heading: He lost his temper, and began again

story.title: Vishvamitra's vow
story.body: Vishvamitra had given up a kingdom to become a sage, and had already started his effort over more than once. Then, tested again, he lost his temper and cursed the apsara Rambha, and with that curse the power of his long austerity was spent. This time he made a vow: he would not give way to anger, or even speak. He kept a long silence. Obstacles came again and shook him, but anger couldn't get in. In the end he reached his goal, and Vasishtha, the rival he had once fought, embraced him as a friend.
story.lesson: Relapses happen. A clear vow and steady practice can loosen anger's grip.

days.for_you: If you've promised yourself before and blown it, you're in Vishvamitra's company. His story keeps going after the relapse.
days.today: Make one specific vow for this week, such as 'I won't send messages while angry', and tell one person.

profile.for_whom: For anger that flares and leaves damage: snapping at people, losing your temper, irritation that builds. Starts where the Gita starts, with what the mind keeps dwelling on.
situations: irritation when things don't go my way
angry when someone blocks what I want
example_notes: I snapped at my kids again and felt terrible afterwards
I lose my temper at work over small things
When I can't get what I want I get really angry
I shouted at my mother and can't take it back
Little things make me furious and I don't know why
Gussa bahut jaldi aa jata hai, phir pachtata hoon

not_for.who: someone angry because they were wronged or treated unfairly
anger at being passed over at work

plans.title: Comparison & self-worth
plans.intro: Krishna says it twice, in chapter 3 and again in chapter 18: better your own path walked imperfectly than someone else's walked perfectly. Around that line sit verses on being your own friend (6.5), contentment free of envy (4.22), dropping the 'I' that keeps score (2.71) and doing your own work as worship (18.46). The last is from the Mahabharata: a half-golden mongoose and the smallest gift at an emperor's sacrifice.

days.heading: Are you on your own side?
days.for_you: Comparison is mostly a voice that pushes you down. Krishna says you can be your own friend or your own enemy, and asks you to lift yourself up. Start by noticing which one you've been lately.
days.today: Each time you compare yourself today, add one line of what you'd say to a friend in your place.

days.heading: Borrowed lives are dangerous
days.for_you: Śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ: your own path, even done imperfectly, is better than another's done well. Comparison quietly swaps your path for someone else's and then grades you on theirs. Krishna calls that swap dangerous.
days.today: Write one thing you want for your life that you'd still want if nobody could see it.
days.note: The verse is about your own nature and calling, whatever role family or birth handed you.

days.heading: Content, and free of envy
days.for_you: Krishna describes someone content with what comes, beyond envy (vimatsaraḥ), steady in success and failure, and free even while working hard. You can keep your ambition and drop the constant glance sideways.
days.today: Mute one account that reliably makes you feel behind, for this week.

days.heading: The 'I' that keeps score
days.for_you: Nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ: without 'mine', without the ego that measures. Peace, Krishna says, comes to the one who moves through life without that scorekeeper. Comparison is the scorekeeper, running all day.
days.today: Notice one moment today when you felt better because someone else did worse. Just notice it.

days.heading: Your own path, again
days.for_you: Krishna repeats 3.35 almost word for word near the end of the Gita, so it can't be missed. Work that fits your nature counts, even done imperfectly.
days.today: Spend 30 minutes on something you're good at that doesn't impress anyone.

days.heading: Your work as worship
days.for_you: Sva-karmaṇā tam abhyarcya: by doing your own work, you can worship the source of all life and find fulfilment. Your work needs no ranking to be an offering. It needs to be yours, done with care.
days.today: Do one ordinary task today slowly and well, as an offering.
days.note: Work as worship never means overwork or putting up with exploitation.

days.heading: Half a golden mongoose

story.title: The mongoose and the handful of flour
story.body: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand horse sacrifice, a mongoose appeared with one side of its body made of gold. It declared that the whole sacrifice was worth less than a handful of flour. Once, it said, during a famine, a poor gleaner and his family each gave their last share of flour to a hungry guest. When the mongoose rolled in the flour that had spilled, half its body turned gold. It had gone to many great sacrifices since, hoping to turn the other half, and none had done it.
story.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

days.for_you: The emperor's ceremony had everything. The family's handful had more. What you do has its own worth, whatever it sits next to.
days.today: Give something small today, time, food or help, that nobody will count.

profile.for_whom: For measuring yourself against others and coming up short, and the anxiety it brings: friends' successes, batchmates placed or settled first, social media, the cousin who is always ahead.
example_notes: My friend got into Harvard and I cried in the bathroom
Everyone my age seems to be doing better than me
I scroll Instagram and feel like a failure
My colleague got promoted and I can't be happy for him
Half my class has jobs lined up and I'm still waiting to hear back
My parents keep comparing me to my cousin
Sab aage nikal gaye, main wahin ka wahin

plans.title: Confusion & hard decisions
plans.intro: The whole Gita answers one undecided man. Arjuna admits he doesn't know what's right and asks for help. Seventeen chapters later, Krishna hands the choice back to him: reflect on all of it fully, then do as you choose (18.63). These verses follow that arc: admitting confusion, seeing why a divided mind can't move, knowing even the wise get confused, what clear judgement looks like, choosing, and acting with evenness. The last is Arjuna's own answer, from sitting down in 1.47 to standing ready in 18.73.

days.heading: Admit you don't know
days.for_you: Kārpaṇya-doṣopahata-svabhāvaḥ: Arjuna says his nature is overcome, he's confused about what's right, and he asks plainly to be taught. Clarity in the Gita starts here, with someone honest enough to say 'I don't know'.
days.today: Write the decision as one question. Then write what you're afraid each answer will cost.

days.heading: Why you keep going round
days.for_you: Krishna says the decided mind is single, while the undecided mind branches endlessly. Each option grows its own what-ifs, and those grow more. That's the loop you're in, and it comes from a mind without a single aim yet. Intelligence has nothing to do with it.
days.today: Ask yourself what you most want this decision to protect. Answer in one word.

days.heading: What clear judgement looks like
days.for_you: Krishna describes clear (sāttvika) understanding: it knows when to go forward and when to hold back, what should be done and what shouldn't, what to fear and what not to, what binds and what frees. That's a checklist. Run your choice through it.
days.today: For each option, answer two questions: does this bind me or free me? What am I afraid of, and should I be?

days.heading: Reflect fully. Then choose.
days.for_you: Vimṛśyaitad aśeṣeṇa yathecchasi tathā kuru. After seventeen chapters, Krishna hands the choice back to Arjuna: think it through fully, then do as you wish. The choice was always his, and yours is yours.
days.today: Set a deadline for this decision and put it in your calendar.

days.heading: Act, and stay even
days.for_you: Once you've chosen, Krishna's advice is to act steadily and let go of clinging, staying the same in success and failure. No decision comes with a guarantee, and evenness lets you act anyway.
days.today: Take the first concrete step on your choice today, however small.

days.heading: Arjuna sits down, and stands up
days.for_you: Arjuna's decision was the hardest anyone in the epic faced. He took his time. He asked, listened, questioned, and then stood up.
days.today: Write what standing up on your decision looks like, in one sentence.

profile.for_whom: For being torn and unable to choose: two offers, stay or leave, a move, a choice with no clean answer. Arjuna's own confusion and the Gita's way through it.
example_notes: I have two job offers and I change my mind every hour
Should I quit my job or stay, I can't decide
We're deciding whether to move back to India and I'm torn
I don't know whether to marry the person my parents chose
Every option feels wrong and I'm frozen
Samajh nahi aa raha kya karun

plans.title: Love and devotion
plans.intro: Bhakti is the warmest thread in the Gita. Krishna says people come to him in distress, in curiosity, in need or in wisdom, and all four are welcome (7.16). These verses walk through his promises: he lives in those who love him (9.29), he lifts them out of the drowning sea (12.7), he gives them the understanding to reach him (10.10). Then they turn to practice: offer everything (9.27), and keep your mind on him, because you are dear to him (18.65). The last is from the Ramcharitmanas, Ram at Shabari's door.

days.heading: Every reason is welcome
days.for_you: You may come to Krishna because something hurts, because you're curious, because you need something, or because you understand. Krishna calls all four sukṛtinaḥ, good people. Whatever brought you here counts.
days.today: Name, honestly, which of the four brings you here today.

days.heading: He lives in those who love him
days.for_you: Krishna holds no favourites and no grudges. Love is the one thing that changes the relationship: those who love him live in him, and he in them.
days.today: Spend two quiet minutes today simply thinking of Krishna, asking for nothing.

days.heading: Lifted out of the sea
days.for_you: Krishna's promise here is personal and quick: acirāt, soon. Whoever rests their heart in him, he lifts out of the sea of birth and death. Devotion in the Gita comes with being held.
days.today: When something worries you today, say his name once and breathe out.

days.heading: Make everything an offering
days.for_you: Krishna widens bhakti to cover the whole day: work, meals, gifts, hardships. Each can be offered to him. Your ordinary day becomes the worship.
days.today: Before one routine task today, offer it to Krishna in a single sentence.

days.heading: You are dear to me
days.for_you: Near the end of the Gita, Krishna makes a promise to Arjuna and calls it true: priyo 'si me, you are dear to me. Devotion runs both ways. He loves you back.
days.today: Light a lamp or sit at your altar today, and read this verse aloud.

days.heading: Ram at Shabari's door

story.title: Ram visits Shabari
story.body: Shabari was an old forest woman who had waited for Ram for years. When he finally came, she washed his feet and fed him the roots and fruit she had gathered, and he praised every bite. Then Ram told her he recognised only one bond, the bond of devotion, and described nine forms of it. The eighth was being content with what comes and never looking for faults in others.
story.lesson: What counts is the heart you bring.

days.for_you: Shabari had no learning or status to offer, only years of waiting and a basket of fruit. Ram said that was enough.
days.today: Offer one simple thing to Krishna today, a flower, a fruit or a little water.

profile.for_whom: For someone drawn to devotion: wanting to feel close to God, to pray with feeling, to love the divine.
situations: want to feel closer to God
example_notes: I want to feel closer to Krishna
I pray every day but want it to mean more
I'm drawn to bhakti and don't know where to start
I feel peaceful when I do puja and want more of that
I want to love God, not just ask for things
Bhakti mein mann lagana chahta hoon

plans.title: Fear of failure
plans.intro: Arjuna's crisis is fear of what his action will lead to. Krishna answers with the most quoted line in the Gita, 2.47: you have a right to the work, never to its fruit. From there the verses show why the result was never yours alone (18.14), why no sincere effort is wasted (2.40), how to stand the same in a win or a loss, and what acting with skill looks like. The last is from the Ramayana, the moment Hanuman is reminded what he can do.

days.heading: The work is yours. The result never was.
days.for_you: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
days.today: Write down the result you're afraid of. Under it, write the three actions that are actually yours.
days.note: Plan and care about results as much as you like. Just keep the outcome from owning you.

days.heading: You are one cause out of five
days.for_you: Near the end of the Gita, Krishna lists what shapes any outcome: the setting, the doer, the means, the many efforts, and daiva, the unseen. You are one of five. Fear of failure quietly assumes you're all of them.
days.today: Take one past failure and name the other four causes. Notice how much of it was never yours.
days.note: You still own your part fully. You are one cause among five.

days.heading: No sincere effort is wasted
days.for_you: Krishna says nothing you begin on this path is lost, and even a little of it protects you from great fear. Honest effort stays with you as skill and steadiness, whatever the result.
days.today: Write one thing an old 'failure' taught you that you still use.

days.heading: Win or lose, stand the same
days.for_you: Notice the order: first steady yourself about the outcome, then act. Winning and losing will still feel different. You can step forward without your worth riding on which one comes.
days.today: Before your next attempt, say: either way, I'll still be me tomorrow. Then begin.

days.heading: Yoga is skill in action
days.for_you: Yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam. Once the fear of the result loosens, your attention comes back to the work, and the work gets better. Skill here means doing the task with your whole mind on it.
days.today: Give your hardest task 25 undivided minutes today. No checking how it's going.

days.heading: Do the work in front of you
days.for_you: Fear often shows up as not starting. Krishna's answer is plain: action is better than inaction, and even keeping the body alive needs action. Do the next piece, ready or not.
days.today: Do the smallest next step on the thing you've been avoiding, before noon.

days.heading: Hanuman at the back of the crowd

story.title: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
story.body: At the edge of the ocean, the search party looking for Sita stopped. One by one, each warrior said how far he could leap, and none could reach Lanka. Hanuman sat quietly at the back. The old bear-king Jambavan turned to him and reminded him who he was: his birth, his strength, everything he had already done. Why are you holding back? Hanuman stood, grew to his full size, and made ready to leap.
story.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

days.for_you: Fear of failure can make you the quietest person in the room. Let these verses, or a friend, be your Jambavan.
days.today: Send one person a message reminding them of something they're good at. Then ask someone to do the same for you.

profile.for_whom: For dread about a result that isn't in your hands yet: an exam, an interview, a launch, a review. The Gita's answer to doing the work without holding on to the outcome.
situations: launching something and fearing it flops
example_notes: My results come out on Friday and I feel sick thinking about it
I have an interview next week and I'm sure I'll mess it up
Launching my product next month and terrified nobody will want it
My appraisal is coming and I keep imagining the worst
What if I fail and let my parents down
I studied hard but I'm scared it won't be enough

plans.title: Gratitude
plans.intro: Krishna tells Arjuna where to look for him: in the taste of water, the light of the sun and moon, the strength in people (7.8). These verses start there, with the ordinary things we stop noticing. Then they ask what we owe back (3.12), find the spark in whatever shines (10.41), and turn gratitude into action: share first (3.13), give well (17.20). The last is from the Ramcharitmanas, a boatman who refused his fare.

days.heading: A spark of something larger
days.for_you: A friend's kindness, a child's laugh, a piece of music that stops you. Krishna says each is a spark of his radiance. Seeing them that way makes the good in your day feel less like luck and more like a gift.
days.today: Name three things that shone today, however small.

days.heading: Give the right way
days.for_you: Krishna's best kind of giving, sāttvika dāna, expects nothing back, goes where it's needed, and comes at the right time. That is gratitude, passed on.
days.today: Give something this week to someone who can't return the favour.

days.heading: The boatman who refused his fare

story.title: Kevat at the Ganga
story.body: Kevat, a boatman, would not take Ram across the Ganga until he had washed Ram's feet, joking that dust which once turned a stone into a woman might turn his boat into one too. Ram laughed and agreed. On the far bank Sita offered her ring as the fare. Kevat folded his hands and refused. He had worked for wages all his life, he said, and today he had been paid in full.
story.lesson: Some things can't be priced, and gratitude can be payment enough.

days.for_you: Kevat counted the moment itself as his reward. Some of your best days will feel like that too.
days.today: Tell one person today, specifically, what they've given you.

profile.for_whom: For when life feels good and you want to hold on to it: health, family, a quiet morning. Gratitude kept as a practice.
example_notes: My family is healthy and I feel so thankful
Life is good right now and I want to remember it
Grateful for my parents and everything they gave me
Things finally worked out and I want to stay humble
I woke up today just feeling blessed
Bhagwan ka shukriya, sab achha chal raha hai

plans.title: Grief & losing someone
plans.intro: The Gita begins with grief. Arjuna sits down in his chariot, unable to face losing the people he loves, and Krishna's first teaching (2.11 to 2.30) is about death: what ends and what does not. These verses stay with that teaching. You can keep grieving while you read them. They give the grief a wider frame: the self that was never born and does not die, worn clothes set aside, the unseen before and after. The last is Bharata in the Ramayana, coming home too late.

days.heading: What was never born doesn't die
days.for_you: Na jāyate mriyate vā kadācit. Krishna's first comfort is about the person you love. What made them who they were, the self, was never born and does not die when the body does. Take in as much of it as you can today, and let it sit beside the grief.
days.today: Say their name out loud today, in a sentence that starts with 'I remember'.
days.note: Mourn fully. This verse is comfort about what remains.

days.heading: Worn clothes, set aside
days.for_you: This is the Gita's best-known picture of death: as we set aside worn clothes for new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body. Krishna offers it to the one grieving. Hold it for yourself, and be careful offering it to someone else in fresh pain.
days.today: If you have something of theirs, hold it for a minute. Let yourself feel whatever comes.

days.heading: Childhood, youth, age, and on
days.for_you: You already watched the person you love change, from a younger self to the one you last knew. Krishna asks you to see death as one more change the self passes through. He says the wise are not bewildered by it. In the first weeks, being bewildered is allowed.
days.today: Look at one old photo of them at a different age. Notice that it's still them.

days.heading: Nothing can touch it
days.for_you: Nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi. No weapon cuts the self, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it. Whatever happened to the body at the end, through illness, accident or age, did not reach who they were.
days.today: If the last days were hard to watch, read this verse slowly, twice.

days.heading: A leaf, a flower, a little water
days.for_you: Krishna says that whatever is offered with love, even a leaf, a flower or a little water, is accepted. Many families remember their dead with exactly these things: water, flowers, a lamp. Love needs somewhere to go, and a small offering gives it a place.
days.today: Make one small offering in their memory today: a lamp, a flower, some water, or a kindness done in their name.

days.heading: Coming home too late

story.title: Bharata returns to Ayodhya
story.body: Bharata was far away at his grandfather's home when his father, King Dasharatha, died. Messengers called him back without telling him why. He rode into an Ayodhya that had gone quiet, went looking for his father, and learned he was gone. He fell to the ground and wept. When he could stand again, the family priest Vasishtha gently told him it was time to perform the last rites, and he did them, grieving as he went.
story.lesson: Missing the goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next.

days.for_you: If you weren't there at the end, because of distance, work or a hospital's rules, Bharata's grief is yours. The Ramayana lets him fall and weep, and then gives him something to do for his father.
days.today: If something is left undone for them, a call, a letter, a rite, choose one and do it this week.

profile.for_whom: For someone grieving a death: a parent, a partner, a friend, someone who mattered. Lets the loss be as big as it is before anything else.
situations: the first anniversary of a death
example_notes: My father passed away last month and I can't believe he's gone
It's been a year since my mother died and it still hurts like the first day
My husband died and the house is so quiet
My best friend died suddenly and I keep reaching for my phone to call him
Papa ke jaane ke baad sab khaali lagta hai
My grandmother who raised me passed away

not_for.who: a breakup or someone who left but is alive
parents who are alive but far away

plans.title: Guilt & past mistakes
plans.intro: Arjuna asks a question many of us ask at night: why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to (3.36)? Krishna's answers are some of the most hopeful in the Gita. Even the worst wrongdoer crosses over on the raft of understanding (4.36). Fire turns wood to ash (4.37). Whoever turns around wholeheartedly is counted among the good (9.30). You still owe others whatever amends are due, and these verses free you to make them. The last is from the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira after the war.

days.heading: Why did I do it?
days.for_you: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
days.today: Write what happened in two sentences, with no adjectives about yourself.

days.heading: The raft across
days.for_you: Krishna says even if you were the worst of all wrongdoers, the raft of understanding would carry you across. Guilt says you are what you did. The verse says you can cross over from it, with the river still there behind you.
days.today: Ask yourself: what did I not understand then that I understand now?
days.note: Understanding frees you to change and to make amends to anyone you harmed.

days.heading: As fire turns wood to ash
days.for_you: Real understanding, Krishna says, burns away the hold of past actions the way fire turns wood to ash. The event happened. Its grip on you, the replaying and the shame, is what can burn.
days.today: If there's a letter you'd write to the person you hurt, write it, even if you never send it.

days.heading: Counted among the good
days.for_you: Api cet su-durācāraḥ: even someone who has done great wrong, once they turn wholeheartedly, is to be counted among the good, because their resolve is now right. Krishna looks at the turn as well as the record.
days.today: Name the turn you're making, in one sentence: from now on, I…
days.note: Turning around includes making amends to anyone you harmed.

days.heading: Soon it becomes who you are
days.for_you: Kṣipraṃ bhavati dharmātmā: such a person soon becomes good and finds lasting peace. Krishna even tells Arjuna to declare it boldly. The change starts as a decision and becomes character through what you do next.
days.today: Do one act of repair today: an apology, a correction, or help given where you once took.

days.heading: Then set it down
days.for_you: Krishna's last counsel in the Gita: take refuge in me; I will free you from every wrong; do not grieve (mā śucaḥ). He says it to a man about to act. Once you've owned what you did and done your part, you're allowed to put the weight down.
days.today: Before sleep, say what you've done to make it right. Then say: I'm putting this down tonight.
days.note: Krishna says this to someone about to act. It lifts fear, and your responsibilities stay with you.

days.heading: He won the war and wanted to disappear

story.title: Yudhishthira after the war
story.body: Yudhishthira won the war and could not bear it. So many of his own family were dead, and he blamed himself. He wanted to give up the throne and go into the forest for good. One after another, his brothers, Draupadi, and the sages Devasthana and Vyasa argued with him about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life. Slowly he agreed to stay and rule, and to spend what was left of his life doing good.
story.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

days.for_you: Running away can feel like the only honest answer to what you did. Yudhishthira's family argue for staying and doing good with what's left.
days.today: Choose one ongoing way to give back that's connected to what happened, and start it this week.

profile.for_whom: For something you did that you keep going back to: a mistake, a hurt you caused, a choice you regret.
situations: a wrong choice in the past
example_notes: I hurt someone I love and I can't stop going back to it
I made a mistake at work that cost a lot and I can't forgive myself
I said things to my father before he died that I regret
I cheated and the guilt is eating me
I keep thinking about how I treated my friend
I wasn't there when my family needed me

plans.title: Lasting joy
plans.intro: The Gita has a clear view of happiness. Some joy starts sweet and turns bitter (18.38). Some starts hard and ends like nectar (18.37). These verses begin with the person who is happy from within (5.24), tell the two kinds of joy apart, show where the lasting kind lives (5.21, 2.65), and end with two practices: choosing the harder joy and keeping a gentle mind (17.16). The last is from the Yoga Vasishtha, a crow who lived through the ages and stayed happy.

days.heading: Lit from within
days.for_you: Krishna describes someone whose happiness, pleasure and light are all inside: antaḥ-sukhaḥ, antar-ārāmaḥ, antar-jyotiḥ. Good days still come from outside. This joy doesn't depend on them.
days.today: Sit for a minute with your eyes closed, and notice anything in you that feels good right now.

days.heading: Why some joy sours
days.for_you: The extra drink, the late-night scroll, the impulse buy. Krishna calls this rājasa pleasure: nectar at first, poison later. Knowing which kind you're reaching for is half the work.
days.today: Catch one 'nectar first' pleasure today before you reach for it.

days.heading: A joy that doesn't run out
days.for_you: Outside pleasures end when the thing ends. Krishna points to a joy inside, akṣayam, one that doesn't run out. It grows the more your happiness rests on yourself.
days.today: Spend fifteen minutes on something that needs nothing bought or scrolled.

days.heading: Clear mind, light heart
days.for_you: Krishna's word is prasāda, clarity or serenity. When the mind clears, sorrow loosens its hold on its own. A lot of lasting joy is a quieter mind.
days.today: Clear one small mess today, a drawer or an inbox, and notice how your mind feels after.

days.heading: Choose the joy that starts hard
days.for_you: Exercise, practice, an honest conversation, a habit you're building. Krishna calls this sāttvika happiness: bitter at the start, nectar at the end. That joy lasts.
days.today: Do one thing today that's hard at first and good in the end.

days.heading: Practise a gentle mind
days.for_you: Krishna calls these the austerity of the mind: serenity, gentleness, silence, self-control, a clean heart. Practised daily, they keep a good mood from slipping away.
days.today: Keep ten minutes of silence today, phone away.

days.heading: The crow who outlived the ages

story.title: Bhushunda
story.body: The sage Vasishtha travelled to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who had watched whole ages of the world come and go and was still happy. Asked his secret, Bhushunda listed his habits. He didn't brood on the past or the future. He didn't fret about what he'd get next. Learning never made him proud. And he was glad when others were glad, and sad when they were sad.
story.lesson: A long, glad life comes from staying present, wanting little and staying kind.

days.for_you: Bhushunda's last habit is the easiest to start: share in other people's joy. It doubles yours.
days.today: Celebrate someone else's good news today, out loud.

profile.for_whom: For a calm, good phase where you want to go deeper: joy that doesn't depend on things going your way.
situations: feeling calm and want to go deeper
example_notes: I feel calm lately and want to go deeper
I'm in a good place and want a joy that lasts
Things are peaceful and I want to understand that peace
Happy without any big reason, want to keep this
Meditation has been helping and I feel lighter
Mann shaant hai, aur gehraai chahta hoon

plans.title: Loneliness & homesickness
plans.intro: Krishna calls himself the friend of every being (5.29) and places the divine in every heart (18.61). These verses are for anyone alone in a new city, far from family, or lonely in a full house. They move from the promise that you're never lost to the one who sees you (6.30), to the list of everything Krishna says he is to us, home and friend included (9.18), and then turn outward: feeling others' joy and pain as your own, and being the friend you need. The last is from the Ramayana, two exiles who swore friendship over a fire.

days.heading: You are never lost to him
days.for_you: Krishna says that whoever sees him everywhere, and everything in him, is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them (na praṇaśyati). Loneliness feels like being lost to everyone. This verse names one bond that distance can't break.
days.today: Step outside for five minutes tonight and look at the sky. The same sky is over home.

days.heading: Someone lives in your heart
days.for_you: Īśvaraḥ sarva-bhūtānāṃ hṛd-deśe 'rjuna tiṣṭhati. Krishna places the divine in the heart of every being, which means in yours, here, in this flat and this city, as much as back home or in a temple.
days.today: Sit quietly for two minutes with a hand on your chest. Just notice that you're there.

days.heading: Home, shelter, friend
days.for_you: In one verse Krishna lists what he is to every being: goal, support, witness, home (nivāsaḥ), shelter (śaraṇam) and friend (suhṛt). If you've been missing all of those, this verse names them together.
days.today: Make your space feel like home in one small way: a lamp, a photo, or a smell from home cooking.

days.heading: The friend of all beings
days.for_you: Suhṛdaṃ sarva-bhūtānām: Krishna is the well-wisher of every being, and knowing this, he says, brings peace. That peace can come on a quiet evening with no calls, because someone wishes you well all the same.
days.today: Call or message someone from home today. Tell them one ordinary thing about your day.

days.heading: Feel their joy and pain as yours
days.for_you: The highest practice, Krishna says, is to feel others' joy and sorrow as if they were your own. Loneliness turns attention inward. This verse turns it outward, and that's often where connection starts.
days.today: Ask one colleague or neighbour a real question about their week, and listen to the answer.

days.heading: Be the friend
days.for_you: Krishna describes the person dear to him as friendly and compassionate (maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca), hating no one. You can't make people reach out to you, and you can be the friendly one first. It counts even when nothing comes back right away.
days.today: Invite one person for tea, a walk or a call this week.

days.heading: Two exiles and a fire

story.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
story.body: Ram had lost his home, and his wife Sita had been taken. Sugriva, driven out by his brother, had lost his home and his wife too. They met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Then Sugriva brought out the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away. Ram broke down at the sight of them, and Sugriva, who had his own grief, comforted him: in trouble, think it through steadily, and lean on your friend.
story.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

days.for_you: Far from home, the friends who matter are often the people who understand what you've lost.
days.today: Find one person who's also far from home and suggest meeting up.

profile.for_whom: For feeling alone: in a new city, far from home, among people who don't really know you.
example_notes: I moved to a new city and don't know anyone
I'm surrounded by people and still feel alone
Living abroad and I miss having people who know me
Weekends are the hardest, I have no one to call
After retirement the days are empty and quiet
Naye shehar mein koi apna nahi hai

plans.title: Losing hope
plans.intro: The Gita's teaching begins at its hero's lowest point. Arjuna puts down his bow and sits in the chariot, unable to go on (1.47). Krishna stays with him. These verses move from that collapse to Krishna's first push to stand, his promise that no one who does good comes to ruin (6.40), the care he offers those who turn to him (9.22), and two practices for days when hope is thin. The last is from the Ramayana: Lakshman sitting with Ram through four months of rain.

days.heading: Even Arjuna sat down
days.for_you: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.
days.today: Tell one person, plainly, that things are hard right now.

days.heading: No one who does good is lost
days.for_you: Arjuna asks what happens to someone who tries and falls short. Krishna answers tenderly, calling him tāta, my dear: whoever does good never comes to a bad end, here or after. What you've tried to do well has not been wasted.
days.today: List three good things you did this year that nobody saw.

days.heading: What you lack, carried
days.for_you: Yoga-kṣemaṃ vahāmy aham: Krishna says he carries what those who turn to him lack and guards what they have. Bills still need paying and plans still need making. The verse invites you to stop carrying all of it alone.
days.today: Hand one worry over, in prayer, to a friend, or on paper, and agree not to pick it up again today.
days.note: Trust eases worry. Keep doing your part and planning well.

days.heading: Be on your own side
days.for_you: Uddhared ātmanātmānam: lift yourself by yourself, and don't push yourself down. In hard times the harshest voice is often our own. Krishna asks you to be your own friend, and Arjuna himself shows that asking for help is part of that.
days.today: Speak to yourself today the way you'd speak to a friend in your situation.

days.heading: With a heart that doesn't give up
days.for_you: Krishna calls yoga the unhooking from sorrow and says to practise it with resolve, anirviṇṇa-cetasā: with a mind that doesn't lose heart. Hope here is something you do. You carry on, a little each day.
days.today: Pick one small daily action and keep it for a week, whatever your mood.

days.heading: Some seasons are for waiting

story.title: Ram waits out the monsoon
story.body: After Sita was taken, the rains came, and Ram had to wait four months on a mountainside before any search could begin. Nothing could be done. He couldn't sleep for grief. Lakshman sat with him and reminded him that endless grieving drains every purpose, and that this was a season for waiting, not for giving up. Ram resolved to wait well, and when the rains ended, the search began.
story.lesson: Some seasons are for waiting. Wait well, without letting grief take you.

days.for_you: If nothing you do seems to move anything right now, you may be in a monsoon. Monsoons end.
days.today: Name one thing to tend while you wait: your health, a skill, or a friendship.

profile.for_whom: For when it all feels like too much and you've sat down like Arjuna did: hope running low after setbacks, but not in danger.
situations: lost the will to keep trying
example_notes: Nothing I try works out and I'm close to giving up
After years of trying I feel defeated
I failed again and I don't know if I can keep going
Everything went wrong this year and I've lost hope
I feel like sitting down and not getting up
Kuch theek nahi ho raha, ummeed khatam ho rahi hai

not_for.who: someone thinking of ending their life

plans.title: New beginnings
plans.intro: Krishna has advice for anyone at the start of something: for the one beginning, action is the way (6.3). These verses take you through a start. Every new thing comes with flaws, like fire with smoke (18.48). With steady effort it's within reach (6.36), so keep doing the work (3.19), cut through doubt (4.42) and step up (11.33). The last is from the Chhandogya Upanishad, a boy who walked off with four hundred thin cows and came back with a thousand.

days.heading: Every start has smoke
days.for_you: Krishna's image is fire and smoke. Every new job, city or project will come with things that don't work. That's normal, and Krishna asks you to keep going when you hit them.
days.today: Write down the first thing that went wrong in your new start. Then write the next step anyway.
days.note: This answers perfectionism. If a place is harming you, leaving can be the right call.

days.heading: Within reach
days.for_you: Krishna is honest: this takes discipline. He's also clear that with sincere effort and the right method, it can be done. New things feel hard because they're new.
days.today: Pick one habit that will make your new start work, and do it daily for a week.

days.heading: Keep doing the work
days.for_you: After the excitement of the first day comes the long middle. Krishna's advice is plain: keep doing what needs doing, well, without obsessing over how it will turn out.
days.today: Do today's work as if it were your first day.

days.heading: Cut the doubt
days.for_you: Arjuna's doubts didn't go away on their own. Krishna tells him to cut them with understanding: get clear on what you know, then stand up. Doubt will visit any new start. You don't have to wait for it to leave.
days.today: Write your biggest doubt about this new start, and one fact that answers it.

days.heading: Step into your part
days.for_you: Krishna tells Arjuna the larger story is already moving, and his job is to rise and play his part well. Starting something new means you've joined something bigger than you.
days.today: Introduce yourself to one person in your new place who will matter to your work.
days.note: Being the instrument still means you choose and answer for what you do.

days.heading: Four hundred thin cows

story.title: Satyakama Jabala
story.body: Young Satyakama wanted to study, but he didn't know his father's lineage. He told the teacher exactly what his mother had told him. The teacher accepted him for that honesty and handed him four hundred weak, thin cows to look after. Satyakama said he wouldn't come back until they were a thousand. He spent years in the forest, and returned with a thousand cows and a mind that nature itself had taught.
story.lesson: Start honestly, start small, and stay with it.

days.for_you: Satyakama began with very little: no lineage, thin cows and a long road. Your start may look small too. What he did next is what counted.
days.today: Set your own 'thousand cows' goal for this new chapter, and write it down.

profile.for_whom: For starting something new: a job, a city, a marriage, a fresh chapter. Hope with the steadiness to see it through.
situations: new chapter after a hard time
example_notes: Starting a new job on Monday and I'm hopeful
We just moved and I want this to be a fresh start
After a tough year I'm ready to begin again
Getting married next month and excited for the new life
Starting college soon and want to do it right
Naya kaam shuru kar raha hoon

plans.title: Overthinking & anxiety
plans.intro: Arjuna said it first: the mind is restless, stubborn and as hard to hold as the wind (6.34). Krishna agrees, then teaches him what to do with it. The first two verses name the loop and where it starts. The next two give the mind somewhere to rest. Two more are practice you can start tonight. The last comes from the Mahabharata, from a woman who slept once she stopped waiting.

days.heading: Even Arjuna couldn't hold his mind
days.for_you: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.
days.today: Notice one loop today and name it to yourself: there it is again.

days.heading: How one thought carries you off
days.for_you: Krishna's picture is a boat with no one at the oar. One thought pulls, the mind follows, and judgement goes with it. Overthinking usually starts small, with one detail you keep going back to.
days.today: When you catch yourself drifting, ask what the first thought was.

days.heading: A lamp where there is no wind
days.for_you: Krishna describes a flame that stays upright. It still burns and still gives light, and the wind around it makes no difference. You can have that steadiness too, for a few minutes at first.
days.today: Sit for two minutes and picture a flame that doesn't move. Come back to it whenever the mind runs.

days.heading: Little by little
days.for_you: The Sanskrit says śanaiḥ śanaiḥ: slowly, slowly. Nobody quiets a racing mind in one evening, and Krishna asks for patience with yourself while it settles.
days.today: Pick one small window today, like the walk to the car or the kettle boiling, and spend it with no input at all.

days.heading: Practice, and letting go
days.for_you: Krishna's answer has two parts. Abhyāsa means coming back to the practice again and again. Vairāgya means loosening your grip on what the mind keeps chasing. You need both, because practice alone can turn into one more thing to worry about.
days.today: Choose one thing you keep replaying. Decide what you'll do about it and when, write it down, and set it aside until then.

days.heading: Bring it back. Again.
days.for_you: This verse expects the mind to wander. Krishna asks you to bring it back each time it does, gently, without scolding yourself. Every return counts as practice.
days.today: Tonight, each time a thought pulls you away from sleep, come back to your breath. Count the returns if it helps.

days.heading: The night she stopped waiting

story.title: Pingala's song
story.body: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira about Pingala, who sat awake one night waiting for a lover who never came. Every sound outside might have been his footsteps, so she kept listening. Late in the night she saw what was keeping her awake. It was her hope that someone else would arrive and settle her. She let that hope go, and she slept peacefully.
story.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

days.for_you: A lot of overthinking is waiting in disguise: for a reply, a result, an apology. Pingala still cared. She stopped making her rest depend on it.
days.today: Name the one thing you're waiting on. For tonight, let it stay unanswered.

profile.for_whom: For a mind that won't switch off: replaying conversations, rehearsing what might go wrong, lying awake with thoughts that loop.
situations: can't sleep because the mind races
checking the phone for bad news
can't stop thinking about something said
example_notes: I keep going over what I said in the meeting and can't sleep
My mind runs through every way tomorrow could go wrong
I lie awake at 2am replaying things from years ago
Every small message from my boss sends me spiralling
Dimaag band hi nahi hota, raat bhar sochta rehta hoon
I overthink every text I send

plans.title: Stress
plans.intro: The Gita is spoken minutes before a war, to a man whose hands are shaking. Krishna knew what pressure does to a mind. These seven verses start with his first lesson, that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. Then come two pictures of steadiness, a lotus leaf and the ocean, and two practical verses on balance and on working with the fever gone. The last is from the Yoga Vasishtha, about a king who found freedom and kept his job.

days.heading: This will pass, and you can bear it
days.for_you: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.
days.today: Write down what's pressing on you. Next to each one, write roughly when it will be over.
days.note: This is about the ordinary ups and downs of life. If someone is harming or mistreating you, act on it.

days.heading: Why stress steals happiness
days.for_you: Krishna lays out a chain. An unsettled mind has no clarity, without clarity there is no peace, and without peace there is no happiness, however good things look on paper. The workload is one part of stress. The other part is a mind with no place to stand.
days.today: Notice where your mind is during the busiest hour today: on the task, or three tasks ahead?

days.heading: Like a lotus leaf
days.for_you: A lotus leaf sits in water all its life, and the water still beads and rolls off it. Krishna uses it for someone who works fully and lets the mess around them roll off. You stay in the pond and keep your surface dry.
days.today: After your hardest conversation today, take one breath and picture the water rolling off.

days.heading: The ocean doesn't overflow
days.for_you: Rivers keep pouring into the ocean and it stays full and still. Demands will keep coming. In Krishna's picture, peace comes from being deep enough to take them in.
days.today: When a new request lands, pause before replying. Let it arrive before you react.

days.heading: Eat, rest, work, sleep: in measure
days.for_you: This is the Gita at its most practical. Krishna tells Arjuna that the yoga which ends sorrow belongs to someone moderate in food, movement, work, sleep and waking. A lot of stress starts as a schedule with no rest built into it.
days.today: Pick one thing to put back in balance this week: a proper meal, a fixed bedtime, or a real break.

days.heading: Act with the fever gone
days.for_you: The Sanskrit is vigata-jvaraḥ: with the fever gone. Krishna still wants Arjuna to fight, and to fight without the heat of 'mine' and anxious hoping. Offer the work to something larger than your worry, and do it.
days.today: Before your next big task, say what it's for beyond you. Then begin.
days.note: Surrender here means letting go of anxious grasping. Your judgement and responsibility stay with you.

days.heading: A king who didn't leave his job

story.title: Janaka on the palace roof
story.body: Walking in his garden one spring, King Janaka overheard hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. When his attendant came to call him to the day's work, he could have walked away from the throne. He didn't. He went back and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutched.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

days.for_you: When stress builds, it's tempting to dream of quitting everything. Janaka kept the same work and held it differently.
days.today: Do one task today the way Janaka would: fully, and without checking for applause.

profile.for_whom: For pressure from all sides: deadlines, demands and a body that never gets to stand down. Steadiness through ups and downs, not escape from them.
example_notes: Too many deadlines and everyone wants something from me today
The pressure at work is constant and I feel wound up all the time
Between office and home I never get a minute to breathe
Exams, assignments and my part-time job are piling up
I am tense all the time, even on weekends
Business is busy and every day is a fire to put out

plans.title: Staying grounded in success
plans.intro: Good news brings its own tests. Krishna's answer is steadiness: the same mind in praise and blame, gold and stone (14.24). These verses start with what success changes, that people now copy you (3.21), and the pride that can creep in (16.4). Then they turn to humility (13.8), the best kind of doer (18.26) and treating everyone as equal (5.18). The last is from the Mahabharata, a king who rose to heaven and fell as a python.

days.heading: People are watching now
days.for_you: Success gives you an audience. Your team, your juniors, your younger cousins all take cues from how you carry it. Krishna says the world follows the standard the best people set.
days.today: Think of one person who looks up to you. What do you want them to copy?

days.heading: Where pride creeps in
days.for_you: Krishna names these so you can spot them early in yourself: dambha (show), darpa (arrogance), abhimāna (conceit). They grow fastest in a good season.
days.today: Notice one moment today when you wanted to be seen more than you wanted to help.
days.note: Use it as a mirror for yourself. It was never meant as a label for others.

days.heading: Gold and stone
days.for_you: Krishna's free person treats a lump of earth, a stone and gold the same, and takes praise and blame alike. Enjoy the win. Just keep your sense of who you are from rising and falling with it.
days.today: Accept today's compliment with a simple thank you, and move on.

days.heading: No need for status
days.for_you: When Krishna lists what real knowledge looks like, the first word is amānitvam: not needing to be honoured. He puts it ahead of everything else on the list.
days.today: Thank one teacher or mentor who helped you get here.

days.heading: The best kind of doer
days.for_you: Krishna's ideal worker is full of drive and enthusiasm, and still doesn't boast or cling. Success and failure leave them the same. Ambition and humility can sit in one person.
days.today: Set your next goal, and tell no one about it until it's done.

days.heading: Everyone gets the same respect
days.for_you: Krishna's wise person sees the same self in everyone, high or low. Treat people the same way after the win as before it, from the CEO to the security guard.
days.today: Learn the name of someone at work you've walked past for months.

days.heading: The king who became a python

story.title: Nahusha's fall
story.body: King Nahusha was so successful that he was made ruler of heaven. Drunk on it, he made sages carry his palanquin and kicked one to hurry him along. The sage cursed him, and he fell to earth as a giant python. Ages later he seized Bhima in the forest, and was freed only after Yudhishthira answered his questions about what makes a person good.
story.lesson: Success can blind anyone. Conduct is what makes a person good.

days.for_you: Nahusha's own warning is the honest one: nobody notices the change while it's happening. That's why good seasons are the time to check.
days.today: Ask someone close to you if success has changed you, and listen to the answer.

profile.for_whom: For when things are going well: a promotion, a win, money coming in. Staying grounded so success doesn't go to your head.
example_notes: I just got promoted and want to stay grounded
My business is finally doing well
I won the award and don't want it to change me
Money is coming in for the first time and I feel different
Things are going great at work
I hit my target this year

profile.for_whom: For burnout: long days for years, running on autopilot, tired in a way sleep doesn't fix, work that has lost its meaning.
example_notes: 14 hour days for years and I feel completely empty
I'm exhausted all the time and sleep doesn't help
Same tasks every day, I feel like a machine
Work and home leave nothing for me, I'm burnt out
Running my business has drained everything out of me
Thak gaya hoon, har din wahi kaam

profile.for_whom: For fear about work and money: layoff rumours, a shaky job, a business that might not make it, bills that don't wait.
example_notes: Layoffs are happening at my company and I can't stop worrying
I think I'm going to lose my job
Sales are down and I don't know how I'll pay salaries

Naukri ka bharosa nahi raha

days.heading: What is right holds you up

profile.for_whom: For being treated unfairly at work: passed over for promotion, credit taken, criticised in front of others, a boss who never values you.
example_notes: My manager took credit for my work in front of the team
I was passed over for promotion again
My boss criticised me in front of everyone
Whatever I do at work is never good enough for him
They promoted someone junior over me
Office mein meri koi value nahi hai

not_for.who: anger that is about their own temper

days.heading: When kindness is read as weakness
You don't have to forgive yet

profile.for_whom: For being hurt by family or someone close: harsh words from parents or in-laws, a sibling's betrayal, a partner who belittles you. Not about forgiving yet.
example_notes: My in-laws taunt me every day
My brother took my share of the house
My mother's words still hurt years later
My husband belittles me in front of others
My sister turned the family against me
Apne hi log sabse zyada dukh dete hain

not_for.who: someone being hit, threatened or controlled

profile.for_whom: For a living loss: a breakup, a divorce, a partner growing distant, someone who left.
example_notes: She left me after five years and I can't move on
My divorce is final and I feel lost
My partner and I live together but feel like strangers
He ended it by text and I keep checking my phone

Breakup ke baad sab adhoora lagta hai

days.heading: No one calls me by my pet name
The worry that spins at night

profile.for_whom: For worry about parents: living far from them, their health, guilt about not being there, homesickness.

days.heading: We act where we find joy

profile.for_whom: For procrastination and lost discipline: knowing what to do and not starting, starting and dropping it, a side project that never moves.
example_notes: I know what I need to do but I just don't start
I keep putting off studying for my exam
My side project hasn't moved in months

profile.for_whom: For craving that never settles: the phone, food, shopping, more money, wanting the next thing and never feeling full.
example_notes: I can't stop scrolling even when I want to sleep
I keep thinking about food all day
